visual_features.distinctive_marks: intricate, swirling, light blue/cyan patterns on the head and body
visual_features.texture: appears smooth with subtle vertical striations on the body

description: The humphead wrasse is one of the top predators of the reef ecosystem, mainly consuming various invertebrate species including the crown-of-thorns starfish. It is very opportunistic, preying on mollusks (particularly gastropods and bivalves), sea urchins, crustaceans, annelids, other fish, and even toxic species such as sea hares, boxfish, and crown-of-thorns starfish. The species is long-lived, with individuals becoming sexually mature at 5-7 years and known to live for around 30 years. They are protogynous hermaphrodites, with some females transitioning to male at about 9 years old. Adults are usually solitary but also observed in male-female pairs and small groups.
population_estimate: Listed as Endangered with a decreasing population trend across its range. Maximum population density is rarely above 20 adults per 10,000 m². The species has been overfished throughout most of its range due to extremely high value in the live reef fish trade. The Philippines, Indonesia, and Malaysia are the three largest exporters, with uncontrolled harvesting of juvenile 'plate-sized' fish for grow-out operations removing hundreds of thousands of individuals from Indonesia alone over multiple years.
habitat: Found on coral reefs in the Indo-Pacific region from the east coast of Africa around the Red Sea to various areas of the Indian and Pacific Oceans. Juveniles are usually found in shallow, sandy ranges bordering coral reef waters. Adults are found mostly in offshore and deeper areas of coral reefs, typically on steep outer-reef slopes, channel slopes, and lagoon reefs at depths of 2 to 100 m. They are usually solitary but also seen in pairs and small groups.
threats: Overfishing for the live reef food fish trade with extremely high retail value
Selective harvesting of juvenile fish for grow-out operations
Illegal, unregulated, and unreported fishing across national borders
Smuggling despite CITES Appendix II protections
Habitat degradation of coral reefs from climate change and pollution
Very slow breeding rates and late sexual maturity (5-7 years)
ecosystem_role: As one of the top predators on coral reefs, the humphead wrasse plays a crucial role in controlling populations of crown-of-thorns starfish and other invertebrates that can damage coral reefs. It is considered an umbrella species: many other species are sympatric with it and have much smaller ranges, so protecting the humphead wrasse's habitat benefits these other species as well. Its foraging behavior helps maintain invertebrate biodiversity on reefs. The species is also known to cooperatively hunt with the roving coral grouper.
human_connection: The humphead wrasse commands one of the highest retail values in the Asian live reef fish trade, especially when caught alive, making it a delicacy in places like Malaysia and Hong Kong. The Philippines, Indonesia, and Malaysia are the three largest exporters, but illegal trade continues despite CITES Appendix II protections. This species has growing value in ecotourism as dive operators recognize it as a charismatic attraction. It also provides ecological services by controlling crown-of-thorns starfish outbreaks that can devastate coral reefs.
what_students_can_do: Support marine protected areas that protect spawning aggregation sites
Learn about sustainable seafood choices to reduce demand for live reef fish
Participate in citizen science programs monitoring reef fish populations
Advocate for stronger enforcement of CITES Appendix II regulations
Educate restaurants and consumers about the endangered status of this species
fun_fact: The humphead wrasse can change its sex from female to male (protogynous hermaphroditism), with dominant females transitioning at about 9 years old
They are one of the few fish that regularly prey on crown-of-thorns starfish, helping protect coral reefs from outbreaks
Humphead wrasses sometimes engage in cooperative hunting with roving coral groupers
Despite being one of the most valuable reef fish, commanding premium prices in the live fish trade, they have very slow breeding rates and take 5-7 years to reach sexual maturity
Recent genetic analysis in 2025 led to the species being moved from the genus Cheilinus to the resurrected genus Crassilabrus
